title: I Used the Costume-Shop Steamer Hours on the Chair Who Left My Gowns

parts.text: I stepped into steam bay at 1:07 p.m. and chair Faye was already using my numbered gowns. The board said: FORTY MINUTES. GOWNS STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-two, wardrobe lead, holding a clipboard that listed our press. Faye shrugged. "Chairs keep the steam." I photographed the board, the booking, and her hem on my steamer. Then I asked for the steamer hours. At 1:15 the wardrobe desk pinged why Faye's hem sat on our steamer. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The wardrobe desk can see Faye's hem in steam bay during our press.

social.video_title: She left her hem on my numbered steamer — Part 1/2
social.description: Costume shop, a chair on my steamer, a forty-minute clock she posted. I logged the hem. Would you have asked for the steamer hours?

parts.text: Faye called it wrinkle checks until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the steamer still. The gowns went back to my numbered rack. Faye ran a slot of their own and told the next chair atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: CHAIRS DO NOT KEEP THE STEAM. I keep our press on a labeled card. Faye brown-bags her hems. The steamer finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Chairs do not keep the steam — Part 2/2
social.description: Steamer hours, numbered gowns, and a second line on the board. Were wrinkle checks ever our press?
